query: For a FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy used as a thin coating on a conventional metal substrate, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs overall wear resistance and microscopic deformation during sliding in the intended high-temperature operating regime? Define a controlled change relative to a baseline coating condition, predict the corresponding directional changes in wear and deformation, state the regime in which those predictions should hold, identify supporting prior evidence, and specify a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: When a FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy coating is pre-treated to refine its near‐surface grain size (via a controlled annealing treatment), the high-temperature sliding conditions will promote dynamic amorphization that forms an ultra‐nanocrystalline surface layer. This layer, in the inverse Hall–Petch regime, shifts the deformation mechanism from dislocation‐mediated bulk flow to grain boundary sliding, thereby reducing both wear rate and friction relative to the untreated baseline coating.
generation.material_initial_state: Standard as-deposited FeNiCrCoCu HEA coating with a relatively coarse grain structure.
generation.intervention: Apply an annealing pre-treatment intended to refine the near-surface grain structure before sliding tests.
generation.conditions: High-temperature sliding wear conditions representative of the intended operating regime (e.g., elevated temperatures under controlled load and sliding speed).
generation.structural_mediator: An ultra-nanocrystalline, dynamically amorphized surface layer formed in situ during sliding.
generation.mechanism: The refined grain structure under high temperature facilitates dynamic surface transformation into an ultra-nanocrystalline state. This state exhibits inverse Hall–Petch behavior, where grain boundary-mediated mechanisms (e.g., grain boundary sliding) dominate over traditional dislocation activity, thereby reducing friction and wear.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline coating, the annealed/refined coating will show a lower wear rate and friction coefficient, accompanied by microstructural evidence (from TEM/STEM) of an ultra-nanocrystalline, amorphized surface layer, and a shift from dislocation-driven deformation to grain-boundary processes.
generation.baseline: An untreated, as-deposited FeNiCrCoCu HEA coating with coarser grains that does not preferentially form an ultra-nanocrystalline surface layer under high-temperature sliding.
generation.boundary: These effects are anticipated only under high-temperature sliding conditions; different tests (e.g., room temperature static or sliding tests) may not yield the same dynamic amorphization or inverse Hall–Petch behavior.
generation.uncertainty: While inverse Hall–Petch behavior and dynamic amorphization have been documented in similar HEAs (e.g., CoCrFeMnNi), the precise magnitude of wear reduction and the extent of the microstructural transformation in FeNiCrCoCu remain to be experimentally validated.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of FeNiCrCoCu coatings: one as-deposited (baseline) and one treated by annealing to induce a finer near-surface grain structure. Subject both sets to identical high-temperature sliding wear tests under controlled load and temperature. Post-test, characterize the surface using high-resolution electron microscopy (TEM/STEM) to assess grain size and evidence of dynamic amorphization, and measure wear rates and friction coefficients.
measurements: Surface grain size distribution and microstructural features (via TEM/STEM imaging)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the annealed coating does not form an ultra-nanocrystalline, amorphized surface layer and does not display statistically lower wear rate and friction coefficient compared to the as-deposited baseline, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text:
Evidence of Inverse Hall-Petch Behavior and Low Friction and Wear in High Entropy Alloys

Abstract: AbstractWe present evidence of inverse Hall-Petch behavior for a single-phase high entropy alloy (CoCrFeMnNi) in ultra-high vacuum and show that it is associated with low friction coefficients (~0.3). Grain size measurements by STEM validate a recently proposed dynamic amorphization model that accurately predicts grain size-dependent shear strength in the inverse Hall-Petch regime. Wear rates in the initially soft (coarse grained) material were shown to be remarkably low (~10–6 mm3/N-m), the lowest for any HEA tested in an inert environment where oxidation and the formation of mixed metal-oxide films is mitigated. The combined high wear resistance and low friction are linked to the formation of an ultra-nanocrystalline near-surface layer. The dynamic amorphization model was also used to predict an average high angle grain boundary energy (0.87 J/m2). This value was used to explain cavitation-induced nanoporosity found in the highly deformed surface layer, a phenomenon that has been linked to superplasticity.Subject terms: Structural materials, Structural properties
